lesson.title: Imparfait vs Composé
lesson.subtitle: Background canvas (imparfait) interrupted by the event dot (passé composé).

hook.title: Weaving Background Canvas (Imparfait) and Event Dot (Passé Composé)
hook.content: The imparfait (-ais/-ait) paints the ongoing background ('I was waiting for the train, I lived in Lyon'), and the passé composé (j'ai vu, il est arrivé) drops the specific event that happened against that background!

footnotes.title: The 'Was -ing When -ed' Formula
footnotes.content: Whenever English says 'I was doing X when Y happened', X is ALWAYS the imparfait (-ais/-ait) and Y is ALWAYS the passé composé!

pattern.title: Ongoing Frame (-ais/-ait) + Sudden Event (avoir/être + Participle)
pattern.content: Combine an ongoing imparfait clause with a completed passé composé clause.
pattern.linguist_note: Aspectual contrast between imperfective background and perfective foreground structures Romance narrative.
pattern.trap_note: Don't put both verbs in the same tense when one action was already in progress and the other interrupted it!

exercises.prompt: Match each half of a past story with its French tense and role:

matching_pairs.german: Background frame: When I was living in Paris...
Ongoing state: I wanted to go out...

exercises.target_answer: Background frame: When I was living in Paris..., Completed event: ...I found this café, Ongoing state: I wanted to go out..., Sudden event: ...but he arrived
exercises.meaning: Quand j'habitais à Paris... (imparfait), ...j'ai trouvé ce café (passé composé), Je voulais sortir... (imparfait), ...mais il est arrivé (passé composé)
exercises.explanation: Imparfait sets the ongoing stage; Passé composé delivers the event.

exercises.prompt: In 'I was waiting for the bus when he arrived', which tense pair is right?
options: J'attendais le bus quand il arrivait
J'attendais le bus quand il est arrivé
J'ai attendu le bus quand il arrivait
exercises.target_answer: J'attendais le bus quand il est arrivé
exercises.meaning: 'was waiting' = ongoing imparfait (J'attendais); 'arrived' = completed event (il est arrivé)
exercises.explanation: Ongoing background takes imparfait; interrupting event takes passé composé.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences match 'Je voulais t'appeler, mais j'ai oublié'?
exercises.german: Je voulais t'appeler, mais j'ai oublié
exercises.meaning: I wanted to call you, but I forgot
renderings: I wanted to call you, but I forgot
I was meaning to call you, but I forgot
traps: I called you because I wanted to forget
I will call you if I don't forget
exercises.target_answer: I wanted to call you, but I forgot
exercises.explanation: je voulais expresses the ongoing past intention, and j'ai oublié expresses the completed slip.

exercises.idea: when I lived in Lyon I saw this film
cues: When I lived in Lyon → Quand j'habitais à Lyon
I saw this film → j'ai vu ce film
idea_parts: background frame → Quand j'habitais à Lyon
completed event → j'ai vu ce film
exercises.target_answer: Quand j'habitais à Lyon, j'ai vu ce film
exercises.meaning: When I lived in Lyon, I saw this film

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: J'avais très faim, donc j'ai pris un gâteau
exercises.target_answer: J'avais très faim, donc j'ai pris un gâteau
exercises.meaning: I was very hungry, so I had a cake
exercises.explanation: Being hungry was the ongoing state (J'avais faim); taking the cake was the action (j'ai pris).
exercises.affirmation: You contrasted J'avais faim and j'ai pris un gâteau cleanly!

summary.outcome: Combine the imparfait (background state) and passé composé (completed event) in two-clause narratives.

use_example.german: Il faisait beau quand nous sommes sortis.
use_example.english: The weather was nice when we went out.

summary.takeaway: Background state = Imparfait (-ais/-ait); Foreground action = Passé composé.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([20] depuis & the Perfect Split): see how Imparfait vs Composé leads directly into depuis & the Perfect Split.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "When I lived in Lyon, I saw this film" in French:
twist.target_answer: Quand j'habitais à Lyon, j'ai vu ce film
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Quand j'habitais à Lyon, j'ai vu ce film" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Imparfait vs Composé.

était.etymology_derivation: être's imparfait — the background tense, the was of a story already in motion.

avais.english_meaning: had, used to have (j'avais / tu avais)
avais.context_translation: I used to have a small car.
avais.etymology_derivation: Imparfait paints the ongoing background setting.

habitais.etymology_derivation: Take the nous stem (habit-) and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

voulais.context_translation: I wanted to talk to you.
voulais.etymology_derivation: Used for ongoing past desires or polite softening ('I was wanting to ask...').

arrivé.etymology_derivation: Late Latin ad rīpam 'to the shore' — to arrive was to land on a riverbank.

vu.context_translation: I have already seen this film.
vu.etymology_derivation: English already owns this participle inside 'déjà vu'!

pris.etymology_derivation: French uses prendre ('to take') for ordering food and drink, just like English 'I'll take a coffee'.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
